title: The King of Comedy ending - reality or fantasy?

commenti.body: It's been a while since I saw it, but I definitely took it as reality. Like the whole movie sets you up to think the guys is only out of his mind, but then he's actually funny so you as the viewer have to decide if it was worth it.

I tend to think it is fantasy. At first I thought it was maybe real but felt it was a bit weird. Then I looked it up and saw some theories and leaned more towards to considering it as not real. The main reason is that it is just impossible for him to become an overnight success and many things in the end seem exaggerated hence it's just a fantasy. Once I realized it was more like just in Rupert's head it had a bigger impact on me. The movie wouldn't be as special if it was real.
I tend toward fantasy because it's exactly what he would fantasise it to be like after what he did. It seemed just too exagerrated and knowingly so to be real in the movie's context.

I recently rewatched it because it’d leave MUBI and it was one of the first movie-movies I watched of my own choice. Back then and now, I still think it being reality is the most sickening outcome. We see all these social interactions that are just uncomfortable. We hear these jokes that just need some more refinement. We see him getting offered a route to success. But instead he takes a fucked up route of abusing the goodwill of the famous people. And then the larger, grander audience swoops in and it ends up not mattering. I think it’s realistic. If a weird new guy came on a show and did mid material and then later on was revealed to be a kidnapper, yeah, I would hesitate a bit if I saw his book in the stores. It’s all about this “There’s no way he’s going to make it”. People are, left and right, just politely telling him to go do other stuff. 

So while yes, it is interpretative, I also do think that the happenings before and the way in which the fantasies were presented, lend themselves towards it being real. We see Jerry stopping by a TV set after he misused the trust of the kidnapper girl, seeing Pupkin doing the show. He could possibly have fantasized this, but I doubt it. The way people are still “mistreating” him, when the police question him for instance also lets me think it’s reality, “Oh you’re the king? Your room is down the hall with a throne” (I’m a bad fucking paraphraser). All his fantasies are usually glowing, deeply rooted in that dominance he wants over Jerry. I think the whole debacle about him being shown is real too. They give in. Right after, with the news bullettin however? Could be pure “in between” by Marty. It lets you think a little about fame, wanting to be famous, sacrifices, nutjobs and what we as an audience would do as an audience. While still being his fantasy, but still real.

Reality for sure given how audiences would eagerly lap up such a bold prank and romanticize "king for a night oer schmuck for life" mindset. It os similar to Eolf of Wall Street ending with Belford attracting even more people at the end of Wolf.

I'm not sure, because in real life I believe people would be obsessed with Rupert. A guy kidnapped one of the most famous late-night comedians and used that to get onto said comedian's show? People would become obsessed with him. But at the same time the ending feels very fantastical in a way, so maybe a mix of both? Either way this movie is still my favorite of all time and will continue to be a movie I absolutely adore.

Yeah. It's the perfect "twist". The whole time, you're yelling at the screen for this inept loser to just work on his material instead of trying to get his foot through every door he sees and obsessing over the one celebrity he ran into... and then it works. He knew better than you all along. It's the perfect takedown of the "who you know, not what you know" reality.

The movie's kind of empty if it's just a fantasy.
